reconciliation.finding: The fresh PDF text and visually inspected pages explicitly use nonnegativity with equality if and only if the vector is zero. Those source statements are correct. Remove the prior audit's claim of positivity slips; strict positivity for nonzero vectors is an equivalent instructional restatement.
For x+2y+z=0, the stated second basis vector (0,2,-1) is outside the plane. Use (0,1,-2); (x,y,-x-2y)=x(1,0,-1)+y(0,1,-2).

The stated assumption m!=n for arbitrary signed integers does not rule out m=-n. Cosine frequencies m and -m define the same function, so orthogonality requires distinct absolute frequencies; handle zero separately. For nonzero frequency, squared norm is pi; constant 1 has squared norm 2pi. The sine/cosine odd-integrand identity remains valid for all integer frequencies.

Oxford uses sum z_i conjugate(w_i), linear in first argument. The chapter convention sum conjugate(z_i) w_i is conjugate-linear in first and linear in second. Thus p_b(x)=b <b,x>/<b,b>; the Oxford-convention equivalent uses <x,b>/<b,b>. Do not transpose these numerators blindly.

The source gives integral x^3(x^2-1/3) from -1 to 1 as 2/7 and a nonzero projection. The integrand x^5-x^3/3 is odd, so the integral and projection of x^3 onto span(1,x^2) are zero. The orthogonal polynomial x^2-1/3 and squared norm 8/45 are correct. Residual squared norm is integral x^6=2/7.

independentChecks.method: Exact SymPy rational integration and matrix arithmetic; these checks supplement source reading, not replace conceptual proof.
independentChecks.complexConventionExample: Under chapter convention b=(1,i), x=(1,1): <b,x>=1-i, <b,b>=2, coefficient=(1-i)/2. Under Oxford convention <x,b>=1-i gives the same projection.

authoringRequirements: For a nonorthogonal basis B, solve Gc=h with G_ij=<b_i,b_j> and h_i=<b_i,x>; do not sum individual projections. Under the conjugate-first convention, c*Gc is positive for nonzero c exactly when columns are independent.
For weighted metric H, G=B*HB and h=B*Hx. H must be Hermitian positive definite; mere symmetric/Hermitian or semidefinite is insufficient for a genuine inner product on the full space.
For dependent generators, the projected vector remains unique while coefficient representations need not be unique. Never take an inverse of singular Gram matrix.
Projection onto the zero subspace is zero; no zero-vector normalization or division by its norm is allowed.

Cauchy-Schwarz equality includes either vector zero and otherwise complex linear dependence. Triangle equality for nonzero vectors additionally requires the scalar relating their directions to be nonnegative real; arbitrary complex phase is insufficient.
Sampling geometry on polynomials requires enough distinct nodes: n+1 distinct points guarantee positivity on degree <=n; fewer may give a nonzero polynomial of zero sampled norm.
Angles from arccos(inner/(norm products)) are real-inner-product geometry. Complex inner products generally require a separately defined convention and cannot be inserted unchanged into real arccos.
Dimension and independence are relative to a specified scalar field: C is dimension 1 over C and dimension 2 over R. Include the zero space with its empty basis.
Use connected vector arrows and actual perpendicular residual geometry. In function geometry, show odd/even parity or function curves, not only generic vector-colored boxes.
